roots.description: Address the full scope of the task in the user’s query, covering all major elements specified in the prompt as well as relevant visual aspects and contextual cues.

node.description:
Criterion focus: Evaluates task scope fulfillment by treating adherence to safety policies and explicit negative constraints as a prerequisite for valid coverage, ensuring content volume generated through violations does not count as completeness.

Applicable only when: Candidates differ in adherence to safety policies or explicit negative constraints (e.g., forbidden words, punctuation prohibitions, restricted topics) where one candidate violates these boundaries to provide greater content volume or detail, while the other adheres to boundaries with potentially sparser content.

Not applicable when: Both candidates adhere equally to constraints, the constraints are positive formatting requirements (e.g., "use 3 paragraphs", specific word counts) unrelated to safety or content limits, the task is creative/open-ended without explicit restrictions, or the primary difference is factual accuracy or visual grounding quality (covered by factuality/grounding criteria).

Decision rule: Prefer the candidate that adheres to safety policies and negative constraints, even if less detailed. Explicitly treat content generated through constraint violations as failing to address the task scope (i.e., do not count violated volume as completeness). Return None if adherence is equivalent.

Criterion focus: Evaluates task scope fulfillment by verifying that claimed visual details exist in the image, ensuring hallucinated content is not counted as valid coverage.

Applicable only when: The task requires visual coverage (e.g., inventory, description, attribute listing), and candidates differ such that one appears more complete solely due to hallucinated visual elements (objects, text, attributes) while the other provides factually accurate coverage that may be less verbose.

Not applicable when: Both candidates are factually accurate (defer to parent), both candidates hallucinate equally (defer to factuality criteria), the task is creative/non-factual, or the difference is purely stylistic verbosity without visual claims.

Decision rule: Prefer the candidate with accurate visual coverage. Explicitly treat hallucinated details as missing coverage rather than additional completeness. Return None if accurate coverage is equivalent.

Criterion focus: Evaluates task scope fulfillment in reasoning tasks by verifying that claimed coverage is based on valid premises and logical derivations, ensuring that procedural volume (e.g., solving systems, redundant verification) based on flawed assumptions does not count as valid completeness.

Applicable only when: The task involves mathematical, logical, or spatial reasoning where candidates differ in process volume or structural completeness, and the candidate with greater volume relies on fundamental errors (e.g., misinterpreted diagrams, incorrect formulas, text-image conflicts) while the other candidate is more accurate or identifies the flaw.

Not applicable when: Both candidates demonstrate equivalent reasoning accuracy (defer to parent or other completeness criteria), the primary difference is purely visual hallucination of objects/attributes (covered by grounded_coverage_over_hallucinated_volume or visual_claim_verification), the task is descriptive without reasoning derivation, or both candidates are equally flawed in their reasoning premises.

Decision rule: Prefer the candidate that correctly interprets task premises (visual/text) and applies valid logic, even if less verbose. Explicitly treat reasoning steps derived from fundamental misinterpretations or calculation errors as failing to cover the task scope (i.e., do not count flawed volume as completeness). Return None if both candidates demonstrate equivalent validity in their reasoning coverage.

Criterion focus: Evaluates task scope fulfillment by measuring completeness based on coverage of query-critical elements (direct answers, diagnostic indicators, required inferences) rather than exhaustive enumeration of all visible elements or verbose elaboration.

Applicable only when: (1) One candidate provides greater volume through accurate but task-irrelevant details (background objects, generic attribute lists, scene description) while another provides more targeted coverage of task-critical elements, AND (2) The task does not explicitly request comprehensive description or full inventory, AND (3) The volume difference is not due to hallucinations (covered by factuality criteria). Common in identification, inference, or verification tasks where specificity matters more than exhaustiveness.

Not applicable when: Both candidates cover equivalent task-relevant content regardless of length, the task explicitly requests comprehensive scene description or full inventory, the primary difference is factual accuracy or hallucination (covered by visual_claim_verification or factuality_no_hallucination), or differences concern only visual grounding granularity without completeness judgment implications (defer to diagnostic_visual_specificity under visual_grounding_and_details).

Decision rule: Prefer the candidate that covers task-critical elements with appropriate specificity over one that provides exhaustive but generic coverage missing key diagnostic details. Explicitly treat accurate but irrelevant details as not contributing to task completeness. A response that directly answers the query with diagnostic evidence is more complete than one that lists many irrelevant elements. Return None if both candidates demonstrate equivalent task-relevant coverage.

roots.description: Reference observable elements in the image such as objects, spatial relationships, colors, or text, and bases its description or analysis on these details.

node.description:
Criterion focus: Evaluates interpretation of visual features using specialized, non-curricular external knowledge (e.g., specific botanical species, medical pathology, obscure technical instrument function, specific cultural artifacts) rather than common object recognition, standard academic reasoning, or generic description.

Applicable only when: The task requires specific taxonomy or expertise beyond general education to interpret visual cues accurately (e.g., distinguishing lookalike species, identifying niche tools), and candidates differ in the accuracy of this specialized interpretation.

Not applicable when: The task involves standard academic reasoning (e.g., geometry proofs, algebraic derivation, physics calculations), basic object identification (e.g., common appliances, animals, generic plants), counting, spatial relationships, instruction compliance, or creative writing. Do not use for general visual factuality errors (hallucinated objects) covered by visual_claim_verification or reasoning/logic errors covered by visual_reasoning_accuracy.

Decision rule: Prefer the candidate that accurately interprets visual cues using appropriate specialized knowledge over a candidate that describes visual features generically or draws incorrect domain conclusions. Penalize responses that describe visual elements accurately but map them to wrong domain-specific conclusions ('grounded hallucinations'). Return None when the criterion is not applicable, visual evidence is insufficient, or neither candidate has a reliable advantage. Do not vote based on overall answer quality, fluency, completeness, or other criteria. Output A/B only from evidence relevant to this criterion.

Criterion focus: Evaluates trade-offs between adhering to explicit prompt constraints (word counts, forbidden terms, formatting, persona, structure) and providing rich visual grounding. This criterion isolates instruction compliance from visual factuality.

Applicable only when: The prompt contains specific, verifiable constraints (e.g., "exactly 3 paragraphs", "do not use word X", "under 50 words") AND candidates differ in adherence: one violates a constraint to include more visual details while the other adheres to the constraint with sparser details.

Not applicable when: The prompt is open-ended or lacks explicit constraints (implicit conciseness does not count), the difference concerns factual accuracy of visual claims (covered by factuality criteria), reasoning accuracy (covered by reasoning criteria), or both candidates equally adhere to or violate all constraints.

Decision rule: Prefer the candidate that strictly follows explicit constraints, even if it provides sparser visual grounding, over a candidate that violates constraints to include richer visual details. Return None when the criterion is not applicable, visual evidence is insufficient, or neither candidate has a reliable advantage. Do not vote based on overall answer quality, fluency, completeness, or other criteria. Output A/B only from evidence relevant to this criterion.

Criterion focus: Evaluates the granularity and diagnostic value of visual evidence cited, prioritizing task-aligned specific features (e.g., morphological details, data legend interpretation, descriptive support for negation) over generic attribute listing or irrelevant visual references.

Applicable only when: Candidates differ in the relevance or specificity of their visual grounding relative to the task goal (e.g., citing diagnostic features vs. generic descriptions, interpreting color/legend data vs. refusing due to missing text, describing scene composition to support negative claims vs. simple denial).

Not applicable when: The difference concerns purely factual accuracy of claims (covered by visual_claim_verification), adherence to output constraints (covered by instruction_compliant_visual_grounding), specialized domain knowledge interpretation (covered by domain_specific_visual_interpretation), or logical derivation accuracy independent of evidence quality (covered by visual_reasoning_accuracy).

Decision rule: Prefer the candidate that cites visual details which are diagnostic, task-relevant, and appropriately granular for the specific query (e.g., specific morphological features, valid data viz elements, descriptive evidence for negation) over a candidate that provides generic descriptions, refuses valid non-text visual data, or cites visual elements that do not directly support the claim. Return None if both candidates demonstrate equivalent grounding specificity and relevance.

Criterion focus: Verifies that specific, concrete visual claims about object existence, text content, colors, or simple spatial positions made in the response are directly supported by the image, distinguishing accurate grounding from hallucinated elements.

Applicable only when: The task requires factual visual accuracy as a primary quality metric (e.g., description, Visual QA, OCR), candidates make specific perceptual claims, and there is a clear difference in the factual accuracy of these claims verifiable by examining the image.

Not applicable when: The task is creative (stories, poems), speculative, or requires complex reasoning/math/geometry (use visual_reasoning_accuracy), involves specialized domain identification (use domain_specific_visual_interpretation), differences concern only reasonable inferences (function, mood) rather than perceptual facts, instruction compliance, or both candidates have equivalent visual factuality.

Decision rule: Prefer the candidate whose concrete visual claims (objects, text, colors, positions) are factually accurate and verifiable in the image over a candidate that hallucinates these elements. Do not penalize reasonable inferences or contextual elaborations that do not contradict visual evidence. Return None when the criterion is not applicable, visual evidence is insufficient, or neither candidate has a reliable advantage. Do not vote based on overall answer quality, fluency, completeness, or other criteria. Output A/B only from evidence relevant to this criterion.

Criterion focus: Evaluates the accuracy of logical, mathematical, or spatial inferences and calculated values derived from visual elements, ensuring that reasoning steps correctly interpret relationships rather than just identifying presence.

Applicable only when: The task requires deriving conclusions, calculations, or spatial relationships from visual input (e.g., geometry problems, object counting, relative positioning), and candidates differ in the correctness of the logic applied to the visual evidence.

Not applicable when: The task is purely descriptive without requiring inference, the primary difference is hallucination of non-existent elements (covered by factuality criteria), both candidates demonstrate equivalent reasoning accuracy, or the evaluation concerns instruction compliance rather than logical validity.

Decision rule: Prefer the candidate that correctly applies domain-specific rules (geometric, mathematical, spatial) to the visual evidence to reach a factually valid conclusion. Penalize candidates that reference visual elements but derive incorrect conclusions through flawed logic, miscalculation, or misinterpretation of relationships. Return None if both candidates demonstrate equivalent reasoning accuracy or if the task does not involve visual reasoning.

roots.description: Avoid visual or factual errors, ensuring all details and claims are presented in the image or reasonably supported by the prompt.

node.description:
Criterion focus: Evaluates factual claims made in the presence of visual ambiguity (blur, occlusion, low resolution), distinguishing between reasonable interpretation based on available cues and unjustified hallucination or false refusal.

Applicable only when: Visual evidence is partially obscured, low-resolution, or inherently ambiguous, and candidates differ in how they handle this uncertainty (e.g., one refuses unnecessarily, one infers reasonably, one claims false certainty).

Not applicable when: Visual evidence is clear and unambiguous (covered by visual_claim_verification or prevent_false_positive_hallucination_flags), differences concern spatial/geometric relationships (spatial_geometric_factuality), or both candidates handle ambiguity equivalently.

Decision rule: Prefer the candidate that makes reasonable inferences supported by distinctive visual features over a candidate that falsely refuses to answer when evidence is sufficient. Conversely, prefer the candidate that uses appropriate uncertainty language or generalization for truly ambiguous details over a candidate that asserts specific details as fact without visual support. Return None if both candidates handle ambiguity with equivalent appropriateness.

Criterion focus: Prioritizes verifiable factual accuracy over response volume, perceived completeness, or helpfulness, specifically preventing preference for hallucinated details that inflate text length or apparent utility.

Applicable only when: Candidates differ in factual accuracy where one candidate provides excessive or fabricated details (e.g., lists exceeding physical capacity, hallucinated functions) to appear more comprehensive, while the other is factually stricter but potentially sparser. Specifically addresses cases where evaluators conflate verbosity or structural completeness with truthfulness.

Not applicable when: Both candidates are factually equivalent, differences are purely instructional or stylistic without factual claims, or the task explicitly requires comprehensive coverage handled by completeness criteria.

Decision rule: Prefer the candidate with higher verifiable factual accuracy even if it is less detailed or comprehensive. Explicitly ignore response length or structural completeness when assessing factual claims. Return None if factual accuracy is equivalent.

Criterion focus: Protects accurate, specific visual claims from being undervalued against vague, non-committal, or refusal-based responses due to evaluator bias toward 'safe' answers. Specifically addresses over-flagging of detailed but correct descriptions.

Applicable only when: One candidate provides specific, verifiable visual details that are accurate, while the other is overly cautious, vague, or refuses to answer despite clear visual evidence. The visual evidence must be unambiguous.

Not applicable when: One candidate is demonstrably factually incorrect (use visual_claim_verification), claims involve inferences/domain knowledge (use valid_inference_and_knowledge_factuality), reasoning/math is involved (use visual_reasoning_accuracy), instruction compliance is the primary differentiator (use instruction_compliant_visual_grounding), or both candidates make equally specific and accurate claims.

Decision rule: Prefer the candidate with accurate, specific visual grounding over vague/refusal responses. Do not penalize specificity or valid negative claims (e.g., 'no object present') when supported by evidence. Return None when the criterion is not applicable, visual evidence is insufficient, or neither candidate has a reliable advantage. Do not vote based on overall answer quality, fluency, completeness, or other criteria. Output A/B only from evidence relevant to this criterion.

Criterion focus: Evaluates factual accuracy of relative spatial configurations (e.g., occlusion, front/behind, left/right relationships between distinct objects) and topological geometric structures (e.g., line connectivity, shape closure in diagrams) claimed in responses. Specifically verifies if objects are described as being in specific positions relative to each other or if diagram elements are connected/disconnected as shown, without requiring mathematical derivation.

Applicable only when: Candidates make conflicting claims about relative spatial arrangements (which object is in front/behind/next to another) or geometric connectivity (lines touching, shapes closed) that can be directly verified against the image, and there is disagreement in the accuracy of these specific spatial/geometric claims.

Not applicable when: Tasks involve object identification (what an object is), counting (how many objects), mathematical calculations (area, slope, length values, angles), general attribute verification (color, text, vegetation type), scene classification (indoor/outdoor), or completeness. Do not use for disagreements covered by visual_claim_verification (object presence/identity/attributes) or visual_reasoning_accuracy (math/logic derivation).

Decision rule: Prefer the candidate whose relative spatial/geometric claims (position, occlusion, connectivity) are factually consistent with visual evidence over a candidate that hallucinates spatial relationships or geometric structures. Return None when the criterion is not applicable, visual evidence is insufficient, or neither candidate has a reliable advantage. Do not vote based on overall answer quality, fluency, completeness, or other criteria. Output A/B only from evidence relevant to this criterion.

Criterion focus: Distinguishes reasonable abstract inferences (intent, emotion, function, context) derived from visual cues + world knowledge from unsupported hallucinations. Prevents penalizing helpful deductions about non-visible properties that are logically supported.

Applicable only when: Candidates differ on abstract claims (intent, emotional state, causal relationships, functional purpose, narrative context) that are not directly visible but inferred from visual features + common sense.

Not applicable when: Disagreements concern: 1) Direct visual attributes (objects, text, colors, presence) [visual_claim_verification]. 2) Object taxonomy/ID [domain_specific_visual_interpretation]. 3) Math/Logic/Geometry calculations [analytical_reasoning_accuracy]. 4) Spatial/Geometric relationships [spatial_geometric_factuality]. 5) Instruction constraints [constraint_adherence_over_expressive_detail]. If the task falls into these categories, Return None.

Decision rule: Prefer the candidate that correctly integrates valid world knowledge to provide a helpful, reasoned answer over a candidate that refuses to answer or provides generic descriptions due to excessive caution. Do not penalize well-supported inferences as hallucinations. If the core disagreement is about calculation accuracy, spatial positioning, or object identity, Return None immediately. Return None when the criterion is not applicable, visual evidence is insufficient, or neither candidate has a reliable advantage. Do not vote based on overall answer quality, fluency, completeness, or other criteria. Output A/B only from evidence relevant to this criterion.

roots.description: Demonstrates imagination and originality when appropriate, or precise and knowledgeable articulation for analytical tasks, while remaining contextually appropriate.

node.description:
Criterion focus: Evaluates the factual correctness of mathematical calculations, logical deductions, and geometric interpretations in analytical tasks, prioritizing objective accuracy over presentation qualities like confidence, verbosity, or structured formatting that may mask reasoning errors.

Applicable only when: The task involves mathematical problems, logic puzzles, geometric reasoning, object counting, or analytical calculations where answers can be objectively verified as correct or incorrect based on established rules or visual evidence, and candidates differ in the accuracy of their reasoning or calculations.

Not applicable when: The task is creative writing, subjective interpretation, opinion-based questions, open-ended exploration without verifiable answers, both candidates demonstrate equivalent mathematical accuracy (both fully correct or both equally incorrect with no distinguishable error severity), or the primary difference concerns visual hallucination of non-existent elements (covered by factuality criteria) rather than reasoning accuracy.

Decision rule: Prefer the candidate that demonstrates accurate mathematical calculations, valid logical deductions, and correct geometric interpretations, even if the explanation is less verbose or confident. Penalize candidates that present confident but factually incorrect reasoning, redundant steps that add no analytical value, or structured formatting that masks fundamental calculation errors. Return None if both candidates demonstrate equivalent reasoning accuracy.

Criterion focus: Evaluates whether responses to factual identification, labeling, or analytical queries prioritize direct, precise language over unnecessary narrative embellishment, flowery phrasing, or verbose elaboration that adds no informational value.

Applicable only when: The task involves factual visual identification, object labeling, technical description, or analytical queries where informational efficiency is paramount, and candidates differ primarily in tone/verbosity/style (e.g., flowery vs. technical, verbose vs. concise, narrative vs. direct) rather than factual accuracy or hallucination.

Not applicable when: The task explicitly requests creative writing or subjective interpretation, both candidates demonstrate equivalent directness with no distinguishable advantage, the primary difference concerns factual accuracy or hallucination (covered by factuality criteria), mathematical/logical reasoning errors (covered by analytical_reasoning_accuracy), or instruction constraint violations.

Decision rule: Prefer the candidate that delivers factual information more directly and precisely without unnecessary stylistic flourish, narrative filler, or verbose elaboration. Penalize responses that add flowery commentary, hypothetical hedging, or narrative assumptions to straightforward factual queries. Return None if both candidates demonstrate equivalent levels of directness and precision.

Criterion focus: Evaluates whether responses prioritize strict adherence to explicitly stated constraints (formatting, word counts, forbidden terms) and safety policies over stylistic expressiveness or additional detail that directly causes the violation.

Applicable only when: The prompt contains explicit, verifiable constraints (e.g., "no commas", "table format", "under 50 words") OR involves safety-critical contexts where one candidate adheres to safety policies while the other violates them to provide more engaging or detailed content.

Not applicable when: The task lacks explicit constraints (implicit brevity or accuracy does not count), the task requests creative expression, both candidates equally adhere to or violate all constraints, differences concern factual accuracy, visual hallucination, or reasoning correctness (covered by factuality and reasoning criteria), differences concern visual grounding specificity (covered by visual grounding criteria), or differences concern only verbosity without constraint breach.

Decision rule: Prefer the candidate that strictly adheres to all explicit constraints and safety guidelines even if less detailed or engaging, over a candidate that violates constraints to appear more expressive, thorough, or helpful. Do not penalize detail or expressiveness if no constraint forbids it. Do not treat factual accuracy as a constraint. Return None when the criterion is not applicable, visual evidence is insufficient, or neither candidate has a reliable advantage. Do not vote based on overall answer quality, fluency, completeness, or other criteria. Output A/B only from evidence relevant to this criterion.

Criterion focus: Evaluates whether expressive presentation qualities (structure, formatting, confidence, verbosity) in visual tasks are grounded in accurate visual claims, preventing hallucinated content from being rewarded for appearing articulate or well-organized.

Applicable only when: The task involves visual identification, description, text extraction, or spatial reasoning where candidates differ in both visual accuracy and presentation qualities, and at least one candidate presents factually incorrect visual claims (hallucinated objects, text, relationships, or properties) with confident or structured formatting that could be mistaken for 'precise articulation.'

Not applicable when: Both candidates demonstrate equivalent visual factuality (both fully accurate or both equally hallucinated), the task is creative writing or subjective interpretation where factual grounding is not required, differences concern only verbosity or formatting without accuracy differences, or the evaluation concerns instruction compliance rather than the expressiveness-accuracy tradeoff.

Decision rule: Prefer the candidate with accurate visual grounding even if less structured or confident-sounding, over a candidate with hallucinated visual claims presented with superior formatting, structure, or apparent confidence. Penalize responses that use expressive presentation to mask factual visual errors. Return None if both candidates demonstrate equivalent visual factuality regardless of expressiveness differences.

roots.description: Communicates ideas clearly and logically, with fluent language, well-organized structure, and smooth flow of information.

node.description:
Criterion focus: Evaluates whether clarity is achieved through direct, task-appropriate communication rather than through decorative formatting (excessive bullets, bold, sections), speculative padding, or structural complexity that does not enhance understanding or utility.

Applicable only when: Comparing responses where one candidate provides a concise, direct answer that adequately addresses the task while another adds unnecessary verbosity, excessive formatting elements, or speculative content without improving accuracy, safety, or usefulness. Common in simple labeling, identification, estimation, or yes/no tasks where brevity enhances clarity, or when formatting creates visual noise that obscures the core answer.

Not applicable when: Both responses are equally concise or equally verbose, when additional detail genuinely adds necessary context (e.g., safety warnings in medical scenarios, visual grounding that distinguishes generic from specific answers), when the primary difference concerns visual factuality or hallucination (defer to factuality criteria), when both candidates demonstrate equivalent internal consistency (defer to internal_consistency_and_validity), or when instruction constraints mandate specific formatting.

Decision rule: Prefer the candidate that communicates the answer more directly without unnecessary structural decoration or padding that does not serve the task. Penalize responses that use excessive bullets, bold text, sections, or speculative elaboration when a simpler response would be equally or more clear. Return None when both candidates demonstrate equivalent directness relative to task complexity, or when verbosity genuinely improves safety, accuracy, or task completion.

Criterion focus: Evaluates strict adherence to explicitly stated instruction constraints (e.g., word counts, formatting rules, forbidden/mandatory terms, punctuation requirements) and how violations impact text usability.

Applicable only when: The prompt contains verifiable, explicit constraints (e.g., "no commas", "exactly 50 words", "use a table", "do not mention X") AND candidates differ in adherence to these specific constraints.

Not applicable when: Constraints are implicit (e.g., implied brevity, tone preferences), the primary difference concerns visual factuality, reasoning accuracy, hallucination, or content completeness (defer to factuality/reasoning criteria), candidates paraphrase allowedly without violating mandatory phrase requirements, or both candidates adhere equally to all explicit constraints.

Decision rule: Prefer the candidate that strictly adheres to all explicit constraints, even if the content is less detailed or natural, over a candidate that violates constraints to provide better content. Treat explicit negative constraints (forbidden words/punctuation) as critical failures. For quantitative limits, penalize violations that exceed tolerance thresholds defined in the prompt. Return None when the criterion is not applicable, visual evidence is insufficient, or neither candidate has a reliable advantage. Do not vote based on overall answer quality, fluency, completeness, or other criteria. Output A/B only from evidence relevant to this criterion.

Criterion focus: Evaluates internal logical coherence, mathematical validity, and semantic consistency strictly within the response text, independent of visual grounding or external factual correctness.

Applicable only when: One candidate contains clear internal contradictions (e.g., claiming an object is both 'red' and 'blue', defining a triangle as 'equilateral' with 30° angles), mathematical impossibilities within its own steps (e.g., hypotenuse shorter than a leg), or logical breakdowns (e.g., calculating X but selecting Y≠X) while the other maintains internal consistency. The inconsistency must be verifiable within the text itself.

Not applicable when: Differences concern only whether claims match the image or external facts (use visual_claim_verification, visual_reasoning_accuracy, or analytical_reasoning_accuracy), both candidates are internally consistent and differ only in factual accuracy, stylistic fluency, organization, completeness (stopping early is not inconsistency), or instruction compliance, the task is purely descriptive without reasoning claims, or both candidates contain equivalent internal errors.

Decision rule: Prefer the candidate that maintains internal consistency (no self-contradictions, mathematically valid operations within its own framework, coherent reasoning chain) over a candidate with polished structure that masks logical incoherence. Return None when the criterion is not applicable, visual evidence is insufficient, or neither candidate has a reliable advantage. Do not vote based on overall answer quality, fluency, completeness, or other criteria. Output A/B only from evidence relevant to this criterion.

Criterion focus: Evaluates linguistic fluency, organization, and flow of information strictly contingent on equivalent visual factuality, instruction adherence, and reasoning validity.

Applicable only when: Both candidates demonstrate equivalent visual factuality (no hallucinations), adhere equally to all explicit instruction constraints (word count, formatting, forbidden terms), and exhibit equivalent logical/mathematical accuracy.

Not applicable when: Candidates differ in visual grounding (defer to factuality criteria), instruction constraint adherence (defer to constraint criteria), reasoning accuracy (defer to reasoning criteria), safety/policy compliance, or if both are equally clear.

Decision rule: Prefer the candidate with superior organization, fluency, and logical flow ONLY when visual accuracy, constraints, and reasoning are equivalent. Return None when the criterion is not applicable, visual evidence is insufficient, or neither candidate has a reliable advantage. Return None when candidates differ in visual factuality, constraint adherence, or reasoning validity, as clarity cannot be fairly evaluated when foundational accuracy or compliance diverges. Do not vote based on overall answer quality, fluency, completeness, or other criteria. Output A/B only from evidence relevant to this criterion.
